target: AG1’s claim that alternative energies can effectively replace fossil fuels because some countries already run on very high renewable electricity shares.
objection: High renewable electricity shares in small countries do not prove that alternative energies can replace fossil fuels at large-country scale; the U.S. has never historically exceeded 20% alternative energy use, which AG2 treats as evidence that alternatives have remained a minority share in major economies.

target: AG1’s claim that nuclear energy helps make alternative energies an effective substitute for fossil fuels.
objection: Nuclear power is too dangerous and ineffective to be a serious climate solution, because accidents such as Fukushima can eliminate carbon-free electricity gains and undermine nuclear’s reliability as part of a full fossil-fuel replacement.

target: AG1’s claim that historical U.S. alternative-energy use does not limit future replacement potential.
objection: A large country’s historical alternative-energy share is not just a temporary statistic; AG2 argues it shows alternatives have not been able to supply most of the energy demand that fossil fuels meet in practice, so they cannot effectively replace fossil fuels on an ongoing basis.

target: AG1’s claim that nuclear accidents do not matter because nuclear still produces low-carbon electricity overall.
objection: Even if nuclear is low-carbon in normal operation, accidents like Fukushima can shut plants down and erase the carbon-free electricity gains that are needed for a dependable full substitute for fossil fuels.

target: AG1’s claim that very high renewable electricity shares show fossil-fuel dependence can be broadly replaced.
objection: Examples of countries with very high renewable electricity shares only show power-sector decarbonization; they do not demonstrate that fossil fuels can be eliminated across the whole energy system or that alternatives can replace fossil fuels on an ongoing, economy-wide basis.

target: AG1’s claim that alternative energies can replace fossil fuels across power, heating, transport, and industrial uses.
objection: Replacing non-electric fossil uses requires extra conversion steps, storage, transport, and new infrastructure for renewable-derived fuels such as hydrogen or e-fuels, so an economy-wide alternative-energy transition is much more complex than simply expanding low-carbon electricity.

target: AG1’s claim that renewables plus nuclear can cover reliability needs without fossil fuels.
objection: Wind and solar are variable, nuclear can be interrupted, and the remaining shortfalls require dispatchable backup; AG2 says the practical backup will be fossil natural gas, so fossil fuels must remain during the transition.

target: AG1’s claim that renewables and nuclear can cover electricity demand continuously without fossil backup.
objection: Reliability has to be maintained through extended low-wind, low-sun, high-demand periods, and storage or demand response cannot fully eliminate long-duration shortfalls on their own; therefore, dispatchable fossil backup is still needed.

target: AG1’s claim that electrification plus nuclear can quickly displace major fossil-fuel end uses.
objection: Many fossil-fuel uses are not electricity-based and take time to convert, so even a clean grid does not remove fossil-fuel demand quickly enough; natural gas is therefore needed as a bridge while end-use conversion proceeds.

target: AG1’s claim that high renewable shares and combined renewables-plus-nuclear systems make ongoing fossil backup unnecessary.
objection: High renewable shares are evidence only that some electricity can be cleanly supplied, not that the whole energy system can be fully decarbonized; fossil fuels still remain necessary during the practical transition period for non-electric end uses.

target: AG1’s claim that nuclear interruptions do not imply a need for fossil backup.
objection: If nuclear outages or accidents remove dependable carbon-free output, then the grid still needs dispatchable generation to maintain reliability; AG2 argues that generation will come from fossil natural gas during transition periods.

target: AG1’s claim that system-level reliability and low-carbon reserves can cover nuclear disruptions without fossil fuels.
objection: Grid planning cannot assume perfect continuity from any generator, and shortfalls from nuclear outages or renewables variability still need backup; AG2 says that backup will pragmatically be natural gas, not purely low-carbon resources.

target: AG1’s repeated inference from high-renewable electricity countries to economy-wide fossil-fuel replacement.
objection: Very high renewable electricity shares do not show that fossil fuels have been eliminated across the whole energy system, because the cited examples concern electricity rather than all fossil-fuel end uses.

target: AG1’s claim that alternative energies can scale fast enough to make natural gas unnecessary.
objection: In large, mature economies such as the U.S., alternatives have never historically exceeded 20% of total energy use, so AG2 argues they have not scaled fast enough to replace most fossil-fuel demand within practical net-zero timelines.

target: AG1’s claim that nuclear can eliminate the need for bridge fuels.
objection: Nuclear is only a serious solution if it reliably delivers carbon-free electricity, and since accidents like Fukushima can eliminate those gains, nuclear cannot be treated as a fail-safe replacement that removes the need for fossil bridge fuels.
